question.text: A block of mass 2 kg is held against a vertical wall by a horizontal force F = 20 N pushing it into the wall, as pictured. The static friction coefficient between the block and the wall is μₛ = 0.8, and the kinetic friction coefficient is μₖ = 0.6. Taking g = 10 m/s², work out the block's acceleration and the friction force that acts on it.
conditions: the 20 N force is horizontal, directed into the wall
static friction coefficient between block and wall μₛ = 0.8
kinetic friction coefficient between block and wall μₖ = 0.6

figure.description: A 2 kg block is pressed against a vertical wall by a horizontal force F = 20 N pointing toward the wall. The wall provides friction on the block with μₛ = 0.8 (static) and μₖ = 0.6 (kinetic).

solution.approach: The push force sets the normal force against the wall; compare the block's weight to the maximum static friction that normal force can supply to see whether the block slides.

steps.text: The block does not accelerate into the wall, so the wall's normal reaction equals the push.
Find the maximum static friction available and compare it with the block's weight.
steps.equation: f(s,max) = μₛN = 0.8 × 20 = 16 N, weight = mg = 2 × 10 = 20 N

steps.text: Since the weight (20 N) exceeds the maximum static friction (16 N), the block slides down, so kinetic friction applies instead, directed upward.
Apply Newton's second law along the vertical, weight down and kinetic friction up.

final_answer.value: The block slides down with acceleration 4 m/s²; the friction acting on it is kinetic friction, 12 N, directed upward.

common_mistakes.text: Using the static friction limit (16 N) as the actual friction force even after checking that the block slides, giving a = 2 m/s² instead of 4 m/s².
Not checking whether the block slides at all and assuming it stays at rest because the wall is rough.
